title: 'Walk the land.' How leaders and managers help learning happen (or not) - 2
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton names two fundamental attributes of learning-focused school leaders: they are driven by improvements in students' learning, and they know their school from the classrooms, not their offices. He argues that being driven means defining success only by actual improvement by actual learners, and that this takes courage because it is harder to show than a new building or curriculum. Borrowing James Rebanks's line that there is no substitute for walking the land, he distinguishes extended classroom presence from ten-minute learning walks. He rebuts the too-busy objection with the arithmetic of his own leadership team's visit schedule, which produced around 300 half-hour visits a term. He draws a parallel with the NHS evidence failure described by Camilla Cavendish, where fridge temperatures were inspected but diagnoses were not.
points: Learning-focused leaders accept a description of success only if it can be linked to real improvement by real learners, which is braver than showing off buildings or resources.
Real evidence about learning comes from walking the classroom land and spending extended time there, since test results arrive too late to act on.
A ten-minute pop-in learning walk is not what learning-focused leaders do; they stay and watch learners.
Visit time is available once leaders count the roughly 100 hours a week they are in school when lessons are not running.
Systems that measure peripheral things, as with NHS fridge temperatures, miss the central question of whether the core work is done well.
quotes: Leaders and managers in the best learning-focused schools are driven by their commitment to make sure that their students get better. Driven is an important word here.
It’s a little like me showing you the new piano I have just bought. It’s easy.

Their bravery is in their choosing to define their school by something complex and not something simple, by something vitally important and not something showy. It’s this bravery that leaves no one in doubt what is at the heart of the school.

But the definition of a learning walk can be very fluid. I have worked with school leaders who will happily come back from a ten minute ‘learning walk’ that consists of them popping in and out of a few classrooms.

We inspected surgeries fridge temperatures (which matters because medicines can go off) and a host of other indicators such as the friendliness of the receptionist. But we didn’t have the data to tell us whether doctors were diagnosing properly, which is what matters most.

I’ll go to the wall believing that if no one walks the land but depends on reports from others, who probably get their information from someone else, leadership can only struggle to exist in any organisation. In learning- focused schools, the land that leaders and managers have to walk often is the classrooms.
